strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Effectively identifies and demonstrates geometric bias in point cloud segmentation for appearance-distinct objects with similar geometry (refrigerators vs. walls, windows vs. coplanar surfaces)

Technically sound methodology: Mahalanobis distance-based matching properly accounts for anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids; preserving point geometry while adding Gaussian attributes is a principled design choice

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluated on 4 datasets with extensive ablations (Tables 7-17); class-wise analysis shows substantial improvements on geometrically challenging classes (+6.0 refrigerator, +7.2 shower curtain)

Thorough empirical analysis: Section B provides compelling justification for attribute selection (Fig. 8), shows GS quality doesn't determine segmentation success (Fig. 10 PSNR correlation), and demonstrates learned features are more discriminative (Fig. 9)
Consistent improvements across benchmarks: ScanNet v2 +0.9 mIoU, ScanNet200 +1.4 mIoU, ScanNet++ +0.8 mIoU, Matterport3D +0.4 mIoU demonstrate generalization
Practical design: Gaussian-free at inference despite augmented training; clear discussion of computational costs and limitations; acknowledges outdoor and sparse-view challenges
Well-executed presentation: Clear writing, effective visualizations (especially Figs. 1, 3, 8), logical flow, and detailed supplementary material enhance reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: Combines existing techniques (Mahalanobis distance, feature distillation, boundary guidance with BFANet's B-S block) without introducing novel concepts; primarily an engineering contribution

Significant practical limitations from GS dependency: Requires pre-computed Gaussian reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K); 22 min/scene for GS optimization plus 27.9 hours per-dataset training; only applicable to indoor scenes with available GS; limits real-world deployment

Modest overall improvements on main benchmarks: ScanNet v2 +0.9 mIoU is incremental; ScanNet200 hidden test underperforms BFANet (35.7 vs. 36.0); instance segmentation gains only +1.7 mAP25; largest gains are on specifically identified challenging classes

Computational overhead contradicts efficiency narrative: Training increases 67% latency and 30% memory; inference increases 21% latency and 74% memory despite 'Gaussian-free' claim being only partially relevant

Questionable component contribution: Table 8 shows semantic boundaries (76.9 mIoU) contribute substantially to the combined approach (77.8 mIoU); Table 9 shows most improvement comes from distillation alone (77.8) with scale/boundary adding marginal gains

Indirect appearance modeling: Claims to address appearance deficiency but doesn't directly leverage point colors; opacity serves as visibility confidence (indirect) rather than explicit appearance cue; appearance learning comes from Sonata pre-training, not Gaussians per se

Dataset-specific tuning limits generalization: Appearance encoder requires per-dataset pre-training from scratch; multiple hyperparameters (r_g=0.06m, k=20, η=0.7) tune per dataset; no cross-dataset generalization analysis provided

Limited failure analysis: No discussion of when method fails or when geometric information should dominate; weak PSNR-mIoU correlation (Fig. 10) not deeply investigated; scene characteristics that benefit most from GS guidance not analyzed

Comparison with most relevant baseline is competitive, not superior: UniPre3D (another GS-based method) achieves 36.0 mIoU on ScanNet200, competitive with G2P's 36.6; some baselines use external pretraining making direct comparison difficult
